subtopic: MAINTENANCE AND OPERATING EXPENSES, WELLAND CANAL
MAINTENANCE AND OPERATING EXPENSES, WELLAND CANAL
speechtext:
1.	Have the maintenance and operating expenses of the Welland ship canal, per vessel transit, increased or decreased since 1959 and, if so, by how much?
2.	What is the reason for such increase or decrease?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MAINTENANCE AND OPERATING EXPENSES, WELLAND CANAL
speechtext:
The St. Lawrence seaway authority advises as follows: 1. Yes, from $339 in 1960 to $1,082 in 1966.
2. The reasons for the increase are: (a) Increases in payrolls and employee benefits arising from collective agreements negotiated in 1959, 1961, 1964 and 1966. (b) Increases in miscellaneous costs reflecting generally increasing prices, including grants in lieu of municipal taxes at prevailing rates, (c) Following a long period during which maintenance had been kept to a minimum, the need to relieve increasing congestion and to keep traffic moving, which dictated a major improvement program, involving both capital and non-capital expenditures, (d) Increasing traffic, characterized by substantially larger cargoes per transit. This dictated a traffic survey by expert consultants to identify critical areas requiring improvements. This survey, which had been substantially completed by the end of 1966, together with the improvement program in (b) above, produced a 35 per cent increase in canal capacity.

speechtext:
1.	From what countries were seasonal farm labourers brought into Canada under mutual agreement in 1966 and 1967?
2.	What were the total number of seasonal workers brought into Canada in 1966 and 1967?
3.	With what countries has the Canadian Department of Manpower and Immigration held direct or indirect negotiations regarding availability of seasonal farm help for Canada?
4.	If Bermuda and the Bahamas have not been included, what are the reasons for their exclusion?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamenfary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: SEASONAL FARM LABOUR
speechtext:
1. In 1966 seasonal farm labourers were brought to Canada from U.S.A. and Jamaica. In 1967 it is expected workers will be coming from U.S.A., Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and Barbados.
2.	The total number of seasonal workers brought into Canada in 1966 was 2,808, with 2,544 from U.S.A. and 264 from Jamaica. The total number of seasonal workers brought into Canada in 1967 so far is 148.
3.	The Canadian Department of Manpower and Immigration has held negotiations with U.S.A., Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and Barbados regarding availability of seasonal farm help for Canada.
4.	The 1966 movement of workers from Jamaica was an experiment. It was decided this year to broaden the experiment to the two next largest source countries in the Caribbean. A wider extension would have imposed excessive problems of administration. But it has been made clear that, apart from the movement organized by governments, the department will co-operate with employers who, through their own arrangements, hire individual seasonal workers in other commonwealth or French Caribbean territories provided they meet the same terms as those stipulated for the organized movement. If the 1967 movement is successful, and such seasonal labour continues to be required in considerable numbers in 1968, a further extension of the source countries for the organized movement will be considered.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MIDDLE EAST-CONSIDERATION OF RESOLUTIONS BY SECURITY COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister bring the house up to date with regard to the discussions at the United Nations? In particular would he say what significance there is in the fact that France is apparently supporting the U.S.S.R. in the current resolution before the security council; and would the Prime Minister say whether consideration is now being given to the creation of an armed force to maintain the equilibrium in those areas in the Middle East that were recently at war?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: MIDDLE EAST-CONSIDERATION OF RESOLUTIONS BY SECURITY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my right hon. friend knows the security council was meeting this morning to discuss the resolution of the U.S.S.R. which would have provided for condemnation of Israel and the withdrawal of her forces behind the armistice lines in force before the conflict began a week ago. I am informed that this resolution did not carry. I think it was voted on just before we came into the house, at about 2.20 or 2.25, but it did not carry. I am not sure of the position taken by France on that resolution. There is no information I have which would indicate that France supported the U.S.S.R., but I will know that in a few minutes.
There has been no discussion yet at the security council about the establishment of a United Nations presence, though there has been a good deal of discussion behind the scenes among the members of the council about the desirability of establishing such a presence in the area at this time. I am not sure what the security council will do this afternoon. There are two other resolutions before the council, one by the United States calling for discussions among the parties concerned looking toward the conclusion of arrangements for the withdrawal of the armed forces and the establishment of peace in the Middle East, and the Canadian resolution, which has been before the council for some days, requesting the president of the council and the secretary general to take the necessary measures to bring about effective compliance with the cease fire.
June 14, 1967

Inquiries of the Ministry
I believe, Mr. Speaker, subject to confirmation-because I do not know what the security council will decide

the council will probably be discussing the United States resolution this afternoon. Whether it would be desirable to bring forward the Canadian resolution for discussion and decision will depend, of course, on developments. It is our view that only after the security council has exhausted its consideration of all these resolutions and any other action it might take would it be appropriate to have a meeting of the general assembly on the subject, as already proposed by the Soviet delegation.

As my hon. friend knows, it was in 1950 I think when there was a tripartite guarantee of the territorial integrity of Israel. That was agreed on outside the United Nations and did not prove very effective in the circumstances.
While I feel, as I am sure my hon. friend feels, it is of vital importance that these four countries should participate in any guarantee, it would be even better if they participated as four members of the security council and of the United Nations. I hope it can be done in that way.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, conceived on December 17, 1965, when the Prime Minister announced an important redistribution of responsibilities among the departments, was born normally nine months later, on October 1, 1966, date of the proclamation of the Government Organization Act.
The estimates which I introduce today, and which relate to the needs of the department as far as staff, buildings, equipment, operating costs, etc. are concerned, therefore reflect the enthusiasm and the vitality, as well as the evolutive character, the future prospects, a philosopher would say, of a body less than one year old.
Mr. Chairman, I do not need to show the importance of the new department. When the


reorganization took place, the most enlightened commentators did that. It is trite to say that scientific research, the optimum use of natural resources, particularly the power sources, are of fundamental importance to the economic development of Canada.
This young department counting, it is true, on the experience of one of its components, the former Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, has begun already to influence the economic policy of the Canadian government and to translate into administrative facts, programs and deeds, the aspirations and good intentions which brought about its creation.

Mr. Chairman, many debates and questions in this house have given me the impression that hon. members are not as much disposed to question the needs of my department's activities as they are to asking whether we are moving as quickly as possible in these vital fields of national concern. So I shall do my best today to demonstrate that this is so and to answer any other questions which hon. members might wish to raise.
At this point I should like to say a few words about each of the main sectors of my department, namely mines and geosciences, mineral development, water and energy. First of all, in respect of mines and geosciences, the principle objective of this sector is to keep up a high level of survey and research in mineral and geosciences so we can learn better the nation's potential mineral resources, provide industry with the data required for discovery, exploration and utilization of the nation's mineral deposits, assist in the planning and development of these resources and contribute to man's knowledge of the sciences of the earth and its contained minerals.
In developing resources the first requirement is good maps, and to this end we expect that the four mile mapping will be completed in this centennial year; that is four miles to the inch, as hon. members certainly know. We will then be able to devote all our attention to the spec'alized maps required to develop resources in various parts of the country. The reconnaissance geological study of Canada is progressing very well, and we expect that the initial mapping will be completed in about five years.
In astronomy, the new Queen Elizabeth II telescope and associated instruments on Mount Kobau are n^w in the advanced stage of planning, as is the associated institute of astronomy on the campus of the University of

British Columbia. I may give that in passing as an example of the co-operation that exists between the department and the universities of Canada.
Studies of gravity effects have always been important in geological studies, but it is now known that they have extreme importance for satellite investigations, and this particular aspect of the department's activity is being stepped up.
The department carries basic studies on metals, mineral processing and mineral extraction. Let me give you some illustrations of that work. The department is carrying out studies on the bacterial leaching of uranium ore, a method which has considerable promise for treating lower grade deposits in Canada and elsewhere.
Another example is the fundamental studies of the characteristics of rocks and how they break-matters of great importance to the mineral industry-that have recently been undertaken on a large scale at the research centre established at Ell ot Lake. Studies have also been undertaken on the addition of small amounts of uranium and gold to allovs in an attempt to improve the characteristics of these alloys, by reducing corrosion, for example. The mines branch also operates a laboratory studying the effects of atmosphere on explosives. These are examples of the practical work which is being done in this sector of the department.
Special investigation of various instruments, their development and their improvement, is a continuing study in the department, including such things as tellurometers which have greatly speeded up our topographic mapp ng by providing a fast and precise way of measuring distances. For the benefit of those of you who winder what a tellurometer is, it is a scientific device for measuring distances with great accuracy by using waves.

The mineral development sector has administrative and economic research responsibilities. For example, that sector issues exploration permits in respect of all minerals in offshore areas south of the sixtieth parallel and in Hudson bay and Hudson strait, as well as in respect of certain minerals in federal lands in the provinces.
Offshore exploration for petroleum continued to be active during 1966, both on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, with the various permit holders carrying out seismic and core-drilling surveys. Needless to say the acreage of offshore exploration permits is considerably greater than the petroleum exploration areas in the western provinces and has tremendous economic importance for the future.
As is well' known, federal jurisdiction over offshore mineral resources has been contested by the provinces, and the adjudication of this question, at least with respect to the western coast, is now pending before the Supreme Court of Canada.
Along with these new tasks this sector, that is, the mineral development sector, is continuing and expanding studies in the fields of mineral economics, mineral commodities, energy resources, resource management, and mine assistance.
The same group also serves as the repository of mineral industry statistics and information. Its functions include acquiring first hand knowledge of mineral industry activity throughout Canada by on-site investigations, from exploration to marketing, and the publication of reports in this connection.
Activities of the group cover regional studies of the Atlantic provinces' mineral economy, including the Cape Breton coal situation; preparation of a digest of the mining laws of Canada; assessment of several mineral projects throughout Canada for which federal support has been requested; and finally participation in international minerals work through such agencies as the United Nations lead-zinc study group, the organization for economic co-operation and development, and the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
I might mention with regard to this last named institution that the department has taken part in the Kennedy round of negotiations which concluded on May 15, 1967. Mr. Chairman, the third sector is that of hydrology.
I need not, I am sure, insist on the importance of water for the economic life and even cultural life of our country. Everyone is aware of the many domestic and industrial uses of water.
Canada has been bountifully provided with water-Providence must be thanked for that -but that does not mean that we have no problems. Indeed, we have several of them: floods, droughts, pollution, conflicts between users, utilization of tidal waters, etc.
My department has been entrusted the task of developing, of defining a national water policy, the task of co-ordinating the federal responsibilities in this field, of improving through research our understanding of hydrological problems, and that of co-operating with the provinces in this field of research as well as in the implementation of programs of general interest.
Federal-provincial co-operation is essential, Mr. Chairman. Assuredly, the main jurisdiction in hydrology is provincial; still, the


federal government, because of its responsibilities in other spheres, namely fisheries transport, trade, defence, public works of interest to more than one province; in those of international relations, agriculture and what not, has obvious responsibilities in this field.
When dealing with water, we are therefore touching upon a field where federal and provincial jurisdictions are shared, where they inevitably overlap. Consequently, federal-provincial co-operation is indispensable.
If the water level of the great lakes drops or if their waters become more polluted, Ontario is not the only province to suffer; Quebec is also affected, for the St. Lawrence is, in a way, its main street.
Therefore, a good Canadian water policy necessarily requires the co-ordination of federal and provincial policies in this field, and even concerted action in many cases.
With the enthusiastic support of my officials, Mr. Chairman, I have tried, since coming to office, to improve the co-operation between the central government and the provinces in this field. For example, our participation in the International Water for Peace Conference held in Washington, with regard to both personnel and the exhibition which took place within the scope of the conference, was really a joint federal and provincial contribution. The future will show the progress that was made.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion a department or branch of a department, to be successful, must have good personnel, a good administrative structure, good legislation, a good research division and good relations with the outside, with the other departments, other levels of government, industry and the public. That is what we have tried to accomplish with regard to hydrology. We have tried to equip ourselves in each of those fields.
A few words, for example, concerning administration. The department had inherited the water resources branch from the department of northern affairs and national resources. It had also inherited the hydraulic research branch and the marine sciences branch from the department of mines and technical surveys. These three elements have been grouped and reinforced and have become the hydrology services, which will now comprise three branches.
First, the inland water branch, second, the marine science branch and, third, the policy and planning branch.

We have hired and continue to hire staff as quickly as the financial resources of the government and of the department will allow us, as well as the human resources of the country. Today's estimates will help us meet our requirements.
In the legislative field, we hope to introduce this fall, the Canadian waters act, whose main purposes would be to promote co-ordination between federal departments as well as a concerted action with the provinces. In this connection, we have consulted with the provinces, and we shall continue to do so, in order to introduce to the house a piece of legislation that will be acceptable by the greatest possible number of people.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

A basic requirement to national water policies and programs, Mr. Chairman, to the establishment of guides and priorities for action and to the development of specific programs, is a Canadian water inventory of supply and demand of water. There have been people asking me or asking the department, will we or will we not export water to the United States, should we provide for the diversion of rivers from area to area? My answer is always the same. I do not know what we are going to do on the subject of export of water to the U.S., but one thing is absolutely certain. Our present responsibility is to find out as precisely as possible how much water we have and as precisely as possible also how much water we are going to need. I feel this is the main responsibility of the water sector at this time, and that responsibility we are going to fulfil as well as we can.
On the supply side of the inventory, we are rapidly expanding our network of stations to obtain data on water quantities, water levels and water quality. Most stream flow gauging stations are operated in co-operation with the provinces, with the provinces paying 50 per cent of the construction costs and a portion of the operating costs. There are now 2,285 of these operating in Canada, that is, gauging stations. There are now also 124 tide gauging stations, 168 water quality stations and a network of ground water and sediment stations. The estimates provide for a considerable expansion of all this network. So you see, Mr. Chairman, by getting this program working we should, within a minimum of time, obtain a good assessment of water supply and water quality.
In so far as water demand is concerned, this is the other side of the picture. Our
DEBATES	1521
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources information on existing demand and potential demand for water in various basins and regions is inadequate for sound policy formation and planning. With the formation of the policy and planning branch in the water sector, studies are planned in co-operation with the provinces to develop and carry out this part of the inventory. Work will be under way soon.
In addition to good personnel, a good administrative structure, good legislation and a good inventory, Mr. Chairman, we also need good research on water in order to provide scientific and technical insights on which to carry out programs. This is particularly true, in my opinion, when we are dealing with the great lakes. The International Joint Commission has fairly recently given us an interim report on the deplorable situation of pollution in lakes Ontario and Erie. In order to cope with the situation, therefore, we are coming up with a major new interdisciplinary water research centre which is going to be called the Canada Centre for Inland Waters at Burlington on lake Ontario, near Hamilton. This centre will provide answers to some of the management problems of the great lakes, and at the same time will provide technical support to water pollution abatement programs throughout Canada. In due course, the research station at Burlington will be useful to both federal and provincial institutions. The estimates provide for a start on building this vital research centre.
The fact that we are busy setting up conditions for action does not mean we are not doing anything. Walking is still the best way to learn how to walk. Although involved in these preparations, the department has been very active and has been doing things. I should like to give some examples of the things we have been doing. We are continuing joint programs in Ontario and British Columbia under the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act. We now have under way new joint studies and working arrangements in both provinces.
In addition, we are undertaking with Ontario a study of northern Ontario waters. We are completing the Winnipeg floodway program and we are negotiating with British Columbia a joint program for flood abatement in the lower Fraser Valley. We hope shortly to join with the three prairie provinces in a major water supply study in the Saskatche-wan-Nelson system. We will be stepping up our federal-provincial programs as fast as the required legislation, institutional arrangements and staff can be supplied. We are thus

1522	COMMONS
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources moving on a number of fronts to meet our new responsibilities to evolve a sound national water program. I used the word "evolve" but I do not like it much. I think we have a national water policy. It may not be as good as every one of us would like it to be, but we have one and we should improve it to make it as comprehensive as possible.
I should like now to say a word about oceanography. Members know that the continental shelf and surrounding oceans have great importance to Canada. It is estimated that about one quarter of Canada's land area lies beneath the ocean. We are developing a strong competence to study and know the continental shelf and oceans surrounding our shores. Recently I visited the Bedford Institute and was very much impressed with the work done there. This knowledge is being employed and will be increasingly employed in support of exploration and development which will have an important impact on the economy of our maritime regions as well as the entire country.
I come now to the fourth sector of the department, the energy sector. The organization of this particular group is not as advanced as the water sector group. Like everyone else, we had to establish priorities. The Public Service Commission has been searching for some time for a possible person to appoint to the position of assistant deputy minister of energy. I hope the appointment will not be delayed too long.
The energy sector is to be responsible for the development of energy policies at the national level. Organizational planning has been based on full recognition of the continuing important contribution to be made in this field by the several crown companies and agencies concerned which are accountable to the house through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. This sector of the new department will assist in the co-ordination of policy advice which is prepared for me in these several agencies. I might mention, however, that there have already been some considerable accomplishments in this field during the brief lifetime of the new department.
Hon. members have been informed of the creation of the Bajr of Fundy tidal power programming board, with the initiative of this department. This is a joint venture of the New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Canadian governments to try to find a feasible, economic and engineering basis for the development of the tremendous resources of tidal power which are matched nowhere else in the world.
fMr. Pepin 1

My department has also picked up the question of a trans-Canada grid for electrical transmission. A federal-provincial committee has met on several occasions and obtained reports from private consultants. I am hoping that the several interested governments will receive a report from this committee in the not too distant future.
e (3:40 p.m.)
Hon. members have been informed on successive occasions of plans for the development on a large scale of the hydroelectrical potential of the Nelson River in northern Manitoba. I expect to make an announcement in the very near future respecting the conclusion of an agreement with the province of Manitoba to this end.
I have tried, Mr. Chairman, to indicate throughout my speech the responsibilities, the realizations and the potentialities of the new Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. However, I should like to point out again that the nucleus of this young department is the former department of mines and technical surveys, with its long experience in research and development as applied to the mineral resources of Canada. This technical skill will remain as the central core of the new department, and we are building around it the special skills we require for developing national policies related to our natural resources. The great advantage we now have is the technical and scientific skilled personnel who are working hand in hand with the specialists who are developing ideas and plans for the national programs. Quite often they are the same people.
Government expenditure on research is growing, and growing rapidly, as it should. The research arm of this department is carrying out investigations directly related to the economic development of the country, and over the years their pay-off has already been substantial. May I indicate two examples. The old maps of the geological survey of the area at Elliot Lake were the basis for development of the whole Elliot Lake uranium project. The processes for extracting the metals from the ores were developed at the mines branch. As another example, our geographers provided the basic information for ARDA and are providing specialized information for E.M.O. Our topographers have made available maps and air photographs required for the assessment and study of our resources.
In general, Mr. Chairman, I think it is right to say that mines and technical surveys, the old department, had been mostly concerned
June 14, 1967	COMMONS
with providing the basic data for industry, for other branches of government, for other levels of government, in order to bring about the maximum resource development in the country. The new Department of Energy, Mines and Resources will, of course, go on doing that but it will do still more. It will be more involved in the development of basic governmental policies and the development of programs in order to bring about maximum use of these resources, and over a much wider area than that covered by the previous department. I hope that these policies will meet with the approval of members of this house.

Mr. Chairman, I think the report of the minister is a tribute to his department. Personally I had hoped that we would hear something of the minister's own views on this very important department over which he presides. In my judgment there is no department of the government that is more important to the present and future development of Canada than the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It can be described as a Cinderella department, and any ambitious young politician who wants to do great things for this country could ask for no higher task than to have in his possession the portfolio that the minister holds.
Just about a year ago, Mr. Chairman, when the bill to reorganize the various departments of government came up for discussion, it was a Conservative proposal that gave the minister the powers he needed to move forward and to take initiative on his own. The minister is quite correct when he says that the old department of mines and technical surveys fulfilled the function of supplying information to all departments of government, and over the years it has done a wonderful job. I have said this before and I repeat it. The men who manned this department were scientific personnel, the type of personnel who are the eyes and ears of the future of Canada.
Today we waited for the views of the minister. One year ago when the reorganization bill was before us, with the co-operation of the opposition the bill was put through in the minister's absence. I asked the minister presiding over the bill certain questions. Because they covered matters which are so important I am going to repeat them today. The minister has apparently not had his attention directed to the suggestions that were made, even though we had a firm commitment from the Minister of National Revenue that they would be.
DEBATES	1523
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources I should like to quote from page 5784 of Hansard for May 31, 1966, where I am reported as follows:
We should like to know what is the minister's policy in relation to the national oil policy on such questions as (a) setting annual targets to industry. We have not had a statement from the minister on this subject for two years now. Then, (b), what is the attitude of the minister toward building a refinery at Quebec, which negates the background of the whole national oil policy? (c) What is his policy on the second oil pipe line to Montreal? (d) What is his attitude toward oil and gas regulations in the north? (e) What are his attitudes with regard to the oil and gas regulations on the continental shelf which are now in existence? These are matters, Mr. Chairman, vital to the whole future of Canada, and we must have a clearcut statement from the minister so that we know where we are going.
The second major question which I want to put before the commitee for the minister to discuss when he makes his statement deals wth the national energy policy. We should like from the minister some statement (a) as to the relations he foresees between the Federal Power Commission of the United States and the National Energy Board of Canada. There is obviously trouble brewing on this front unless there is a clearcut policy to avoid the difficulties ahead. Then, (b) we also want from the new minister a statement on the national transmission grid, which is vital to the whole concept of sovereignty and using our energy as a basic part of strengthening our bargaining power in the field of resource use on the continent, (c) We shcu'd like a statement from the minister with regard to the relationship between atomic power and hydro reserves in Canada, (d) We should like projections on what the minister foresees is the energy demand for new industrial complexes in Canada during the next 20 to 30 years.
The third subject, Mr. Chairman, deals with water policy, (a) We desperately need something which has been recommended since 1962, and that is a study on the suply of water in Canada.
The minister mentioned something about this and I will come back to it.
I can go into detail on this, but that is sufficient to indicate the subject, (b) Even more importantly, we need a study of the demand.
The minister also mentioned this today and I will come back to it too.
If we have to use United States figures and translate them into figures showing Canadian use, this is a little embarrassing when we are trying to estimate our demand for water. Before we can discuss water intelligently we have to know the supply and demand picture. Then, (c), we should like from the minister officially in his new capacity a statement on the NAWPA plan which the United States has proposed and has been pushing on the legislators of this country in private sessions. And, (d), we should like a statement from the minister on the Kiernan plan proposed by a Canadian engineer. We should like the direction of the minister on these subjects.
There, Mr. Chairman, is a list of about 12 subjects, on two of which we got partial answers today. You can understand the deep

Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources distress of those of us who had something to do with first giving Canada an awareness that our future depends upon the development of the resources of this country in a rational and logical manner.
9 (3:50 p.m.)
The Conservative party formed the government in June, 1957. I became a minister on August 22, 1957. On February 12, 1958 the government announced a development policy for Canada. It took us about eight months to prepare what this government has been unable to prepare in four years. This is a matter most vital to the whole future of this country. It is the basis for the future jobs of unborn generations. We have had a report about what a fine job the department is doing. I accept that and I praise it wholeheartedly. But where does the minister stand? I remind the minister that when the bill was passed it was the Conservatives on this side of the house who proposed the amendment to the bill which gave him some power. These are the terms of the amendment which was introduced on behalf of the government by the Minister of National Revenue:
8Bfl) In carrying out his responsibilities under Section 8A, the minister may formulate plans for the conservation, development and use of the resources specified in that section and for research with respect thereto, and with authority of the governor in council and in co-operation with other departments, branches and agencies of the government of Canada, provide for carrying out such plans.
We wanted to hear about such plans, but what have we heard? Continuing:
(2)	The minister may co-operate with the provinces and with municipalities in formulating and carrying out any plans under subsection (1).
Today we heard a little about this in regard to the Saskatchewan-Nelson system and one or two others. We started these projects but they are still in the planning stage. It continues:
(3)	In carrying out his duties and functions under this section, the minister may consult with and inaugurate conferences of representatives of producers, industry, the universities, labour and provincial and municipal authorities.
These amendments were accepted by the government. Their purpose was to give the minister some power or to create some means by which the minister could use the initiative of the federal government to build this nation. One and a half years later what do we hear about these plans? Very little. There have been studies about this and about that.
I remind the committee about some things that are well known but about which we have to remind ourselves on every occasion. We live on this continent with the great United States of America. They also conduct studies. I hold in my hand the five volumes of the Paley report of 1952 which warned the president of the United States of that day that the United States was running short of strategic items to maintain its industrial complex. Every one of the shortages that the report warned would exist between 1952 and 1980 represented an opportunity for Canada. Because of this report the Conservative government in 1957-58 was able to come up, at short notice, with a national development plan to take advantage of the opportunities for Canadians. Since then a more sophisticated report in the United States has been made, known as "Resources in America's Future". The subheading is: "Patterns of Requirements and Availabilities." The authors are Hans Landsberg and others. The report deals with projected needs from 1960 to the year 2000. The projections, which are maximum, minimum and average, show all the possibilities that may happen to forestry, water resources, minerals, and what have you. The United States knows what it is short of and what it must do to meet its needs.
On the other side of the ledger, what has been done in Canada? The only substantial action we have taken was to hold a conference in Montreal in 1961, known as the Resources for Tomorrow conference. I hold in my hand the first of the four volumes of the report which points the way that the government must follow. There is no lack of suggestions in these four volumes about what we must do to preserve and better utilize our renewable resources. The conference was very general in its outlook but it did point out objectives.
In sheer desperation the people in the private sector tried to bring about some sort of analysis of Canada's resources. I hold in my hand a book entitled: "Canada: An Appraisal Of its Needs And Resources". It is written by Canadians, by George W. Wilson, Gordon and Judek. These professors, helped by grants, put out a tim'd, gentle little appraisal which went up to the year 1975, eight years from now. These men performed a task that should have been performed long ago in Canada. Their timid, gentle approach to our needs only points out the urgency of doing something to carry out the suggestions made by the Resources for Tomorrow conference.

June 14, 1967

I intend to propose two ways in which we can act, and I put forward my propositions in the way I do for the simple reason that I have grave doubts that the government intends to act.
Private enterprise has ample reason to wish to know what the future is for its products. Private enterprise in the United States uses the Landsberg volume to guide it in its projections, as do one or two companies in Canada also. This is my proposal. In the amendments that were included in the bill of last year the minister was given certain powers. Why do we not ask private enterprise, which makes money out of our resources, to conduct research in this field? Perhaps a group of companies could to it. The Conservative government amended the Income Tax Act to allow any group of companies or an individual a 150 per cent exemption on income tax for resea "ch-not a 100 per cent exemption for the expenses for this type of research work but 150 per cent. Second, we amended the Combines Investigation Act to allow companies to combine legally if they did so for research purposes. With the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act there is no reason for the minister, in using his responsibilities as a minister of the crown acting on behalf of the people of Canada, not to call groups of our private companies or enterprises together to ask them to do this research work which is so financially advantageous to them.
The private sector need not deal with the water segment of research; it need only take the commodity segment. It could take the Gordon commission report of 1957 as a starting point. It is true that that report is seven or eight years out of date, but it is a starting point. It could be used in conjunction with the Wilson-Gordon book which gives projections up to the year 1975 A.D. Even if the studies are considerably in error, even if they are followed by more sophist'cated studies later, if they could include optimum projections varying from the most pessimistic to the most optimistic, they would be of great help.
In saying these words I have in mind an example about which I have spoken in this house before. In 1958 when I was the minister responsible for resources I realized that within seven or eight years, if we did not develop more zinc and lead production in western Canada, we would be forced to import lead and zinc into western Canada. Here we were, a nation with bountiful lead and zinc resources, and private enterprise was not meeting its responsibilities. Apparently our boards
DEBATES	1525
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources of directors could look ahead only for a couple of years. If some of them look ahead for five years they think they are being bold and imaginative.
The government did not fail in its responsibilities. We were the ones who put up the guarantee for Canadian National Railways to build a railway to Great Slave Lake. Today there is a mining operation there, which means we need no longer import lead and zinc into western Canada. Not only are we earning exchange dollars for our country but we have added tremendously to the wealth of this nation. The C.N.R. will get all its money back and receive a profit on the money it borrowed. The company which developed the mine will be paying taxes to the federal treasury next year at the rate, I would expect, of between $12 million and $15 million a year. When you show initiative, when you show you know what you are talking about, when you can push private enterprise into making money and when the treasury will get $15 million a year without spending a nickel, that is good, dynamic government. The word "dynamic" does not describe the present government. If private enterprise will not give us the required commodity output even though it is in its own interest to do so, then the government will have to induce or push them into action.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is not just an inventory of our resources which is needed. We need a projection of the demand and a projection of the supply in relation to every commodity. Canada undoubtedly is a resource nation and will continue to be one for many years to come. But though we have been a resource nation from the very beginning, there has never been developed in this country a resource philosophy which dominates the thinking of ministers of finance, which dominates the thinking of governments. If our future depends on the use made of these resources, then the whole organization of tax laws should be orientated to this end. Agriculture is one of our great resources. But there has never been a clearcut understanding in Canada by ministers or by governments of the fact that agriculture is not just an orphan to whom a few crumbs are thrown every so often but an important source of wealth which should be so planned and used as to bring the maximum return to our people and serve the world as a result of the ability of our land to produce.
The same is true of our mining industry. We look on it as a means of raising taxes, providing a certain amount of employment
June 14, 1967
1526	COMMONS
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources and bringing in a certain number of dollars in foreign exchange. We do not look on it as a vital part of the whole economic structure of our country. Our economists use the great ideas of Lord Keynes. Lord Keynes developed a system of economics designed to suit a homogenous, integrated country such as the United Kingdom, a country which was an exporter of manufactured goods and an importer of raw materials. He developed this economic system as a means of avoiding the ups and downs of the economic cycle. We in Canada have transferred this doctrine to our own country without taking account of the fact that Canada is not a homogenous or even an integrated country. We are a country of regions. We are not a sophisticated, mature industrialized country yet. Nevertherless our policies at the national level assume we are all in the same boat. We are not. So if we find two provinces threatened with inflation and eight provinces stagnating, we seek to cure the inflation in two provinces by imposing the same restrictions on the whole country, Whether all parts need it or not.
The whole concept of fiscal, monetary and trade policies fails because governments have failed to accept our need for a resource philosophy. What percentage of our resources should we sell abroad in our best interest? What percentage should we process in Canada in our best interest? Certainly we cannot process them all. This is what I mean by a resource philosophy. It must be apparent from the actions of every minister that he understands it. That is the test. Having sat in this house for four years waiting for some sort of leadership, I confess I am at a loss to find evidence of any. The 60 days of decision petered out into stagnation. Then we saw the reorganization of the government. I can honestly say of the present government that they are great at setting up structures. We have heard more structures described to us today than I have heard in this house in ten years. They are great at setting up structures but are wholly lacking when it comes to action. They fail to realize that when a structure is set up there has to be a brain, there has to be a will at the head of that structure, someone who can think and act. This is what is lacking. The government sets up beautiful structures and mans them with the most competent people they can find. But they lack the brain; they lack the will at the top. They are like a leaderless group. All I can say is: dear Lord, how long must we endure?
fMr. Hamilton.]

I am glad the minister has accepted the fact that we need to study the extent of our water resources. I suppose the best figures we have are those produced by the Resources for Tomorrow conference in 1961. When I hear the minister talking about the need for water it occurs to me that it is important to know not only the extent of the supply but the extent of the demand both now and in the future. I often wonder whether he has referred to the article by Mr. D. Cass-Beggs in volume 1 of the conference background papers. On page 184 appears an estimate of annual water consumption in the principal regions of Canada. The author notes that in 1956 consumption of water in Canada amounted to 10 million acre feet in round figures. He predicts that by 1990 it will have risen to 56 million acre feet.
Why talk in generalities when here is a person who has done the projection? I admit the author had to make his projection by interpolating United States figures. But it appears we have a projection for an increase in water consumption from 10 million acre feet in 1956 to 56 million acre feet in 1990. Whether these figures are entirely accurate or not is beside the point. They are something we can talk about. With all this talk about water, I wish the minister would be a little more definite. Otherwise he may frighten the Canadian people half to death. How much water have we got to meet the expected demand?
The water resources branch of the government has tabulated our river flows and arrived at a total of 2.5 million feet per second based on minimum flows. This works out to 1,620 billion United States gallons of water a day. Translate this into acre feet and we have an indication of our capacity. As a rough yardstick of comparison let us compare our situation with that in the United States. If we have 1,620 billion gallons a day, they have about 650 billion gallons. I should make it clear that the estimate of 650 billion gallons is based on flows of realizable water from surface waters in the United States. Let us take our figure of 1,620 billion gallons a day and reduce it by half. Then consider that today in Canada we are using 10 billion or 12 billion gallons of water a day. We have 800 billion gallons a day to meet that demand. So there is no need for the Canadian people to be terrified for a few years yet.
June 14, 1967	COMMONS
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Naturally we are not likely to give this water away. What attitude was taken by ministers of the crown while Canadians were being assaulted during the last two years by requests from the United States for water. Incidentally, I am glad to hear that these have now been abandoned. Where were the ministers of the crown to defend the Canadian interest by telling the Canadian people and the American people what the United States authorities were asking? They were asking for 120 million acre feet a year under the NAWPA plan. What is the value of an acre foot of water? To my knowledge only one quantitive study has been made. It appears in the Landsberg report at page 385, and is dated 1963. It is estimated with regard to New Mexico, a completely water deficient area:
-an acre-foot of water used for municipal and industrial purposes engendered over $3,000 of total economic product (a combination of primary value-added and value-added by purchases).
If you want to put this into a simple phrase, the value of an acre foot of water for municipal and industrial purposes is $3,000 a year, The report continued:
For recreation the range was from $200 to $300 and for agriculture the range was from $40 to $50.
Thus, an acre foot of water is worth over $3,000 a year in industrial production. Yet the Americans had the colossal gall to come to us and ask for 120 million acre feet a year. Let us forget about the recreational and agricultural values for a moment. One hundred and twenty million times $3,000 is $360 billion a year. This is what the Americans were asking. This shows how generous some people can be with other people's wealth. I never heard a minister of the crown give these figures to a Canadian audience or to an American audience. It is the duty of a minister to defend, and to point out the facts so that the Canadian people will not be robbed of their heritage.
There are many questions I would like to ask and the 12 points I listed a year ago still remain unanswered. I have read the reports of the standing committee which met last year when the new department was being formed, and I have many questions to ask on energy and all these other matters but time does not allow. I would think this committee might be well advised, in view of the importance of the department with which we are dealing, to ask all the questions that should be asked, and to do this we need a longer day than a Wednesday. We in the opposition are

I hope the sense of responsibility of the minister will be such that he will go to his house leader and ask that the committee get another chance to deal with the estimates of his department.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to pay a very hearty compliment to the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle on the excellent speech he has just made. I might take advantage of an inadvertent slip of the tongue on his part when he mentioned a leadership mob to say that his speech should give him a good start.
As was mentioned by the hon. member we should have much more time to deal with this most important department of government. But since we do not I will confine my remarks to one particular policy of the minister and the government.
I wish to protest against a government policy which has brought a certain situation in Canada to a crisis stage. This policy might best be described as fawning, craven subservience and, at the worst, possibly a clandestine conspiracy. Of course, Mr. Chairman, I am speaking about the government's policy or lack of policy with regard to a vital resource and industrial lifeline of Canada, natural gas and gas pipe lines and the vacillating of the government in that regard.
I do not want to go into the pros and cons of the north line versus the south line. This question has been debated at great length in the house without much change in opinions or positions on either side, but I think it would be worth while to review briefly just what has caused the present situation. To do this I have to go back ten years when a policy was being determined in this field by the House of Commons, at that time we had a very strong policy. Whatever else may be said about the late C. D. Howe and his cohorts, nobody at that time denied the strength of their policies when they decided on them. Indeed, many people who were familiar with the situation in those days must now wonder that we can look back on that Liberal government and

It was the government of Hon. Leslie Frost at that time. What did we see happen after a few years went by? First of all we had the National Energy Board meekly and mildly warning about the developing shortage of natural gas in eastern markets. Unfortunately that is about the only role the National Energy Board is empowered to play, to warn meekly and mildly, and to issue licences when people make applications.
For reasons which became only too apparent later, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines deliberately ignored the growing shortage in eastern markets. There was an ignoring or unawareness on the part of the present government of the situation that was developing. I do not care which it was. Both are a condemnation of a government that is supposed to have the interests of the country at heart.
Finally we had the blackmail attempt by Trans-Canada to rush everything through at a moment's notice in order to enable them to have their cake and eat it too. Then we saw the first reaction of the government, the only good reaction I can recall it having in the past


four years, but unfortunately the reaction lasted for only five weeks. The government was unable to resist the pressures brought to bear on it and did an about-face. But it lapsed once more into its familiar role of vacillation, the role of the innocent and helpless bystander, the role of a meek observer of vital decisions having far reaching effects on the country it was elected to protect.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The government said, "Let Trans-Canada decide, let the federal power commission decide, let anybody decide so long as we do not have to make a decision as to what we should do." Unfortunately the minister was the epitome of this tragedy of government on the unhappy day when, in reply to a question as to when we might expect a decision, he rose, shrugged his shoulders and said, "I wish we knew". In fairness to the Ontario government I should say that they had a death-bed repentance. Finally, after bitter debates arose in this house and across northern Ontario and Queens Park, they stirred themselves to raise their voice along with others and decided to make an intervention with regard to this problem.
I say we have had enough delay in respect of this matter. If we look at the Globe and Mail of May 25 last we will see the following in a big write-up about this situation:
Testifying before the commission last month, N. John McNeill, Trans-Canada vice-president, indicated that the company would require a decision on its application for certification of the Great Lakes project by the end of May.
In the event no decision was forthcoming by that time, or the ruling was unfavourable, Trans-Canada would have no alternative but to proceed with its plan to loop sections of its existing line east of Winnipeg to assure the supply of additional gas for Ontario and Quebec next winter.
Panhandle's application for renewed hearings of the Great Lakes scheme may well be rejected by the commission but such a ruling by the F.P.C. would almost certainly be cited by the company as one of its grounds for challenging the legality of any F.P.C. decision in favour of Great Lakes if Panhandle resolves to take it to the courts.
This situation certainly should be clear to anyone who is interested in this matter and who has followed it through the newspapers over the past year. Everyone should have been able to realize that no decision could be made by the end of May. We see now that no decision was made by the end of May. Today, in the middle of June, still no decision has been made. The crisis is growing. The markets are getting shorter and shorter.
In yesterday's Globe and Mail we find further comment on this same subject. From an
June 14, 1967

article by Bruce Macdonald I read the following:
The decision by the Federal Power Commission on Trans-Canada Pipe Line Ltd's proposal for a new natural gas line to eastern Canada via the United States-expected this week-may confront the troubled company with yet another dilemma.
There appears to be a reasonable possibility that the application on behalf of Great Lakes Transmission Co. may be approved with an important condition attached deleting all the current provisions for net export in the United States, which in turn would raise important questions about the economic feasibility of the entire project.
The final paragraph reads as follows:
Given these circumstances, Trans-Canada might find itself iorced either to scale down the 34-inch line it had originally planned to build through the United States or to abandon the southern link altogether in favour of looping the existing Canadian line east of Winnipeg.
This points out in an all too startling and clear manner just what a tremendous hoax has been played on this government over the past year and a half. They reversed a decision on the basis of a comparison that was made at that time and now, a year and a half later, we find that the facts and circumstances given at that time had no relation to the actual situation. It was all part and parcel, as I said, of a blackmail attempt to stampede this government into making an agreement which would benefit one particular company and neglect the interests of the Canadian people almost from coast to coast.
I do not know whether it is necessary to repeat the reasons for the necessity for action to be taken immediately with regard to this burning problem. Certainly, however, this has been pointed out to us almost daily in our newspapers. The government and the country are being reminded of the desperate and growing need for gas in eastern Canada so that the industries we have already built up will continue to operate. Unless immediate action is taken there will be a curtailment of work and production because we have vacillated, waited, played silly games and have dene everything except what we should be doing.
There is no need to repeat again that a building boom would generate all along the course of the twin pipe line. I do not care particularly whether Trans-Canada follows the present line, which probably would be the quickest and least expensive way to get gas to the east, or whether it follows the other proposed line roughly along the route of highway 17. I believe that the build ng of that line would be in the best interests of Canada as a whole because it would open up another vast
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources region of what is potentially the richest part of Canada.
I might remind the government again of the industrial potential that the line would bring to the affected areas. The government pays lip service to looking after the north and is prepared to put people on welfare and declare designated areas and regions. But when there is something which would build up the country they vacillate for four years when they should have been doing something. Most important of all, if we proceed and proceed now to keep this vital resource carrier in this country, we will at least maintain the ability to make Canadian policy in Canada rather than place ourselves at the whims of a foreign body in a foreign country. Surely the lessons of the past year should have been sufficient to prevent us placing ourselves in this very vulnerable position.
So, Mr. Chairman, I say we have had enough procrastination; we have played enough games. The government should instruct the National Energy Board not later than next Monday to grant this licence and get on with this job which we have delayed far too long.

Mr. Chairman, there are three matters I should like to discuss briefly with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. First I should like to commend the minister for his attitude and in many cases his realistic approach to some of the problems facing him in the mineral and energy development fields as well as those fields relating to water conservation and utilization. I think the minister has performed a good service for Canada in attempting to deal with these matters realistically and progressively.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The three matters that I want to discuss are, first, oil markets, second, the extension and addition of pipe lines to deliver natural gas to eastern Canada and to the eastern or central United States and, third, coal exports from the Crowsnest pass area in Alberta and British Columbia to the west coast.
I will deal first with oil markets. We are apprehensive and deeply concerned about what is being done to expand the markets for Canadian oil, particularly oil from Alberta. I am sure the minister is aware of the fact that Alberta's petroleum production has dropped to slightly over 30 per cent of its total capacity, even with the application of good conservation practices, and this of course does not include a significant amount from the tar sands. We do not believe this to be a fair or
DEBATES	1531
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources realistic level of marketing, at least until we have reached the stage where the production of petroleum in Canada is equal to its consumption in this country. We believe a balanced level will be achieved when the total production of petroleum in all of Canada equals the total consumption of oil. This is not the case at present. We know that the market area extending eastward from Montreal is still being supplied by offshore oil. We think that Canadian producers have a right either to supply this market or an equivalent market some place within continental North America. There are a number of reasons for this. One of them is that petroleum should and could be a great asset in earning foreign exchange, and at the present time I understand that Canada is in a deficit position in balancing its exports and imports.
We would like to hear from the minister what he has been doing to expand the availability of markets for Canadian oil, particularly in what is referred to as the Chicago loop. A few days ago the minister was in Washington. When he came back he told the house that he had had some discussions with secretary Udall, but that is all he said. He did not say whether there was a favourable response to his suggestions, whether the United States government was going to encourage this sort of arrangement, or what further action the Canadian government intends to take. All we heard was that the minister was interested-and we are pleased to hear it-and that he had conversations. He did not say anything about the subject matter of the discussions and the response he received. We think it is important for the province of Alberta and for the national economy that some action be taken. We have heard many words, plans, discussions and utterances of good intentions, but we have had no action yet and we think the time has come for the minister to give us at least his impressions of what he expects will happen on the basis of his discussions with the United States officials.
With regard to gas delivery from western to eastern Canada, it is becoming increasingly urgent that some decision be taken to provide additional capacity to deliver gas to eastern Canada. Some complaints have been made about the government's unfortunate decision some months ago to reject the National Energy Board's decision regarding the Great Lakes development, following which some time was lost. I am not too critical of the government in this respect because it saw the light and changed the cabinet order. However, the major problem here is loss of time. All these considerations have to be taken into account.
What has been overlooked by those people who favour the Great Lakes route as opposed to the looping of the present line of the construction of another one a little farther south is that that line would not supply any gas to add.tional customers in the eastern United States. There is a market there for Canadian gas which would benefit not only the Canadian economy but also that of the province of Alberta. So we believe that the government should do what it can to encourage an early decision by the federal power commission. It should do everything to expedite a decision in th s matter so that this line can be built and the looping of the additional pipe line installations in northern Ontario can be proceeded with.
I wish to turn now to my last point, the matter of coal. I am very critical of the manner in which the Canadian government has handled the transport of coal from southwestern Alberta and southeastern British Columbia. However, my criticism does not extend to the minister because I do not think anyone would be justified in criticizing him for carrying out his responsibilities through the national coal board by setting up and providing facilities for the expansion of coal mining in the Crowsnest Pass. I do not believe that this action should be criticized. However, it seems to me that the Canadian

Pacific Railway is being unreasonable and unjust and that the government has been unable to take a positive stand with regard to the railway company's demands for higher rates to transport this coal.
According to the Minister of Transport, both the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance have a direct responsibility to ensure that if there is even the slightest possibility of a subsidy being given to the transport companies, the variable costs of that transportation plus the mark-up are not unreasonable. A cost study has been made on behalf of the coal operators in the Crowsnest pass by a very competent firm of cost analysts. They came up with a figure of $2.86 for the variable costs. So far as we know, and I should like the minister to explain this to us, the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has a complete monopoly on railway transport in the area, has never offered to haul the coal for less than $5.28 a ton until the volume is well over a million tons. They adamantly refuse to enter into any kind of deal for less than that. I do not believe that is being reasonable. I do not believe it is a justifiable charge on the Canadian treasury to be paying a subsidy which in effect means an 84 per cent mark-up of variable costs. This statement is based on the figures we have that the rate would be $5.28.

It may be difficult for the minister and his department to establish these costs. However, I believe we have a responsibility to get on with the job of establishing, first of all, the methods and techniques that are used in establishing the variable costs. Then we can apply these methods and techniques to the problem of transporting coal from Coleman, Blairmore, Michel and Natal to the Pacific coast. This has not been done yet. We, as members of parliament, and the Canadian taxpayers are going to be faced with paying a subsidy.
In my estimation one cannot criticize the intent in entering into this kind of deal in order to get inning operations going I think there is a very bright future for coal mining operations in the Crowsnest area in view of the market in Japan and other offshore markets if we can arrive at transport arrangements to the west coast at a reasonable rate. The minister has partly met this problem, but I believe we also have a responsibility to make sure the raTway companies do not gouge the taxpayers in their demands for

rates. Therefore I want to make it clear to the minister that we appreciate the co-operation he has given to the coal board in making these arrangements with the Coleman collieries. I believe there are others pending.
I also think that if the industry is going to have a long term future on a sound basis the coal must be moved on the basis of a well established variable cost plus a reasonable mark-up. Then the railway will not need a subsidy at all. It is the belief of more knowledgeable people who have studied this situation that the Canadian Pacific Railway can transport this coal at a reasonable rate and still make a profit. We know that the Great Northern offered to haul it for $4 per ton and, according to some of these people, even at $4 per ton there was a profit. This rate is supposed to be the average for hauling coal in the United States.
Under the arrangement that has been made the Canadian Pacific, even after the total volume reaches a million tons from Coleman or two million tons from the area, is demanding $4.60 per ton. Then, of course, there will be no subsidy paid. This figure, as far as we can tell from the studies that have been made, is still too high and represents an unreasonable mark-up in variable costs.
I plead with the minister to have a conference with the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance so that they can go ahead and do what the Minister of Transport promised to do, have a public hearing to establish the methods and techniques used in connection with setting variable costs. A hearing of the interested parties could then be held to determine what the variable costs are after the methods have been determined. This has not been done, and it needs to be done. In every case in the past where the railways have been challenged by competent people, these so-called variable costs have been analysed and a great service has been done for the people of Canada. The time is past due when this needs to be done in so far as variable costs for moving freight are concerned, particularly on heavy commodities.
In closing my remarks I want to say again that we appreciate the attitude shown by the minister in approaching this problem. We wish him well. I hope he will give us additional explanations with regard to the three matters I have raised.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to enable private owners to derive a minimum income from or obtain a certain guarantee on their dwellings.
Every human being is anxious to own a home. Who would venture to suggest it is unreasonable for anyone to wish some day to own a home for his family?
In this country, private property is closely connected with the family. Private ownership is an undeniable natural right that all members of this house, I am sure, or at least, I hope, have their heart set on protecting.
On the other hand, that same private property is a heavy financial burden for the Canadian labourer, for the Canadian worker and, more generally, for the Canadian citizen.
Owning a home is no problem for a family head who earns $8,000 or more a year. But we know that salaried Canadians earn, on the average, less than $4,000 a year, without hope of any increase, either because the industry for which they work cannot develop or because the worker who grew up during the depression does not have many diplomas.
In any event, despite professional training obtained after 15, 20 and 25 years of experience in a given field, very often employees are limited by salary ceilings. This situation is often found among labourers and also among white collar workers in industry and trade, and even civil servants. Those workers who once felt they possessed a certain security when they acquired their homes are now in serious difficulty because in addition to the income tax they have to pay many other real and hidden taxes, new or higher taxes, excise tax, federal and provincial sales tax.
All these taxes imposed by higher levels of government were the main reason for the higher cost of living. That rise in the cost of living created real problems for our municipal and school officials, because all the services rendered by those intermediate bodies
[The Chairman.]
are more and more costly. Indeed, home owners who once could pay up their school and municipal dues with as little as $150 a year, are now faced with the obligation of expending between $450 and $500 a year for the same services. That unforeseen rise in the essential services is reflected in the fact that a great many nice private properties are put up for sale.
Mr. Speaker, in its war against poverty, the Canadian government recently decided to spend an additional amount of money in order to lower as much as possible the cost of rents in the poorer quarters of Montreal, and I take this opportunity to commend the government for that humanitarian action.
It is proven that it is very well to throw a rope to a drowning man but, to my mind, it would be better to build a guardrail at the right spot at the right time to prevent drowning.
True, without government help, many Canadians would be deprived of everything, but it should be recalled that many Canadian families deprive themselves, for in the case of the head of a family, the expenses are a lot heavier when he has a wife and children.
If we look at the income of an unmarried person earning $4,200 per year, we see how the income tax exemptions for married persons are far from balancing the family budget.
For instance, the unmarried person who earns a salary of $4,200 pays an income tax of approximately $475, after a deduction on $1,000, which leaves a net income of $3,725.
The head of the family earning $4,200 pays $128 in taxes each year after benefiting from a deduction of $2,000 for himself and for his spouse, and a deduction of $1,150 for the three children, if we suppose that he has one aged 19 who is a student, one of 14 and one of 8.
The 14-year-old child receives an allowance of $8 a month, or $96 a year. The 8-year-old child has an allowance of $6 a month, or $72 a year. That adds $168 to the income, which then amounts to a total of $4,368 a year-$4,368 less $128 tax, which brings it to $4,240.
The net income of a father of three children of 19, 14 and 8 years old is $4,240 after payment of $128 income tax. The single person having the same salary of $4,200 has a net income of $3,725, after payment of $475 income tax.
